defaults.inclusion_rule: A framework is listed if it ships a first-party or officially documented MCP adapter. Nothing is excluded on quality grounds.
defaults.order_rule: Alphabetical within language group. No ranking is implied or computed.
defaults.version_policy: Era 0 is the release actually measured. Surrounding releases come from the package registry (PyPI, npm) and are shown as not yet measured until a scan covers them.
defaults.green_rule: A cell is 'y' only if the value is present in the tool definition at that framework's declared capture boundary. Nothing else counts.
defaults.partial_rule: 'a' means the capability is not present unchanged: the note must say whether it was transformed at the boundary, only partly preserved, or retained elsewhere by the framework.
defaults.note_rule: Every 'a' and 'n' cell must carry a #n note reference naming the exact mechanism, so a status can be checked rather than trusted.
defaults.usage_rule: No adoption weighting is published. We have no defensible source yet, and an invented percentage would be the least trustworthy number on the page.

coverage.note: The feature surface of MCP 2025-11-25. Derived from the 2026-07-28 catalogue and that revision's official changelog, which enumerates every addition, removal and deprecation relative to this revision. This file is the denominator: what the protocol defines, independent of what we have measured.
omissions: Skills over MCP is not listed. The spec index advertises it, but /extensions/skills/overview 404s and the only published material is a working-group charter, so there is no wire contract to measure against.

Features removed in this revision (initialize, ping, logging/setLevel, resources/subscribe, notifications/roots/list_changed, Mcp-Session-Id, SSE resumability) are absent by design. They belong to the 2025-11-25 snapshot, not this one.

additional-properties.title: `additionalProperties`
additional-properties.description: Controls whether an object accepts keys that are not declared in its properties map.
additional-properties.question: Is each object's additional-properties policy preserved at the capture boundary?
additional-properties.notes: Four measured capture boundaries preserve the source policy. CrewAI's generated args_schema changes additionalProperties on the root and nested object schemas.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: Pydantic model generation rewrites additionalProperties on several object boundaries, changing whether undeclared keys are accepted.

verdict.headline: Preserved at four boundaries, changed at one.
verdict.detail: CrewAI rewrites the policy while the other captured definitions retain it.

additional-properties.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP tool schemas declaring additionalProperties.
known_issues: A changed policy can make a downstream caller reject valid extension keys or send keys the server rejects.
additional-properties.why: Object openness is part of the parameter contract. Changing it can alter which calls validate before they reach the server.

arrays-of-objects.question: Do arrays of structured items survive to each capture boundary?
arrays-of-objects.notes: Measured as present at every declared framework capture boundary.

default-value.title: `default`
default-value.description: Documents the value a server or client should assume when an optional parameter is omitted.
default-value.question: Is the declared default value preserved at each capture boundary?
default-value.notes: Every adapter now hands the agent the source default of 20. CrewAI rewrote it as recently as crewai-tools 1.14.7; the generated args_schema preserves it at 1.15.1.

verdict.headline: Preserved at all five boundaries.
verdict.detail: The default survives every adaptation measured here. This row changed when CrewAI moved from 1.14.7 to 1.15.1, which is the kind of silent repair that only shows up if you keep re-measuring.

default-value.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP tool schemas declaring default values.
known_issues: A changed default can cause a caller and server to assume different behavior for the same omitted argument.
default-value.why: Defaults communicate omission behavior. Losing or changing one can alter calls without changing the visible parameter type.

description-fidelity.question: Is the full tool description present at each capture boundary?
description-fidelity.notes: Four frameworks pass the description through byte for byte. One rewrites it into a longer template.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the captured description is rebuilt as `Tool Name: ... Tool Arguments: {schema} Tool Description: ...`, duplicating the schema as prose and parameters.

verdict.headline: Verbatim in four frameworks, rewritten in one.
verdict.detail: One framework rebuilds the description to include the tool name and the full argument schema.

destructive-hint.title: `destructiveHint`
destructive-hint.description: An MCP tool annotation the author sets to declare that a tool is destructive, it deletes data, is irreversible, or has a large blast radius. It lives in the tool's `annotations` object alongside readOnlyHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint.
destructive-hint.question: Is the destructive marker present at each capture boundary?
destructive-hint.notes: The annotation is absent from all five declared capture objects. LangChain and Pydantic AI retain it elsewhere in framework metadata; CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Mastra drop it. No v0.1 renderer captures a serialized provider request.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the adapted tool object exposes no annotations field, so the value is not recoverable after adaptation.
notes_by_num.2: LangChain: retained on `StructuredTool.metadata`, but absent from the OpenAI-compatible dictionary produced by `convert_to_openai_tool`.
notes_by_num.3: OpenAI Agents SDK: `FunctionTool` keeps `_mcp_title` only; the behavioural hints are not carried.
notes_by_num.4: Pydantic AI: retained in `ToolDefinition.metadata['annotations']`; not part of `parameters_json_schema`.
notes_by_num.5: Mastra, `mcpMetadata` carries the server name and version only; annotations are not attached to the tool.

verdict.headline: Absent at all five declared capture boundaries.
verdict.detail: Two frameworks retain it elsewhere; three drop it during adaptation. Final provider requests were not captured.

destructive-hint.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers declaring this annotation. Not estimated, the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
known_issues: A policy layer reading retained metadata in LangChain or Pydantic AI sees a value absent from the captured tool definition; those two integration surfaces can disagree.
Because the annotation is absent rather than false, a consumer cannot distinguish "not destructive" from "never told".

after: : no annotations field exists in this format

destructive-hint.why: A guardrail reading only the captured tool definition receives no structured destructive signal. Two frameworks still hold the value where an application policy layer can read it; three do not. This measurement does not claim what a later provider request contains.

enum.question: Are the allowed enum values present at each capture boundary?
enum.notes: Measured as present at every declared framework capture boundary. Where a framework builds its schema from a model class, optional parameters are wrapped, but the constraint remains inside the wrapper.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: preserved inside the `anyOf` wrapper emitted for optional fields, so the constraint sits one level down rather than being lost.

verdict.headline: Present at all five declared capture boundaries.

enum.why: If it were lost, a downstream model could pass values your server rejects, producing a failed call the agent must recover from.

nested-objects.description: An object typed parameter carrying its own nested properties.
nested-objects.question: Does nested structure survive to each capture boundary?
nested-objects.notes: Nested input survives everywhere measured. A reference based encoding is an equivalent representation, not a loss.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: nested types are re expressed via `$defs` and `$ref`. Semantically equivalent, so mcp-mirror resolves the reference before comparing rather than reporting it as flattening.

null-acceptance.title: Null Acceptance
null-acceptance.description: Distinguishes an optional parameter that may be omitted from a parameter that explicitly accepts null.
null-acceptance.question: Does adaptation preserve whether each parameter accepts null?
null-acceptance.notes: Four capture boundaries preserve the source nullability. CrewAI wraps optional fields in unions that newly accept null.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: optional fields are emitted through nullable anyOf wrappers, broadening the accepted values beyond omission alone.

verdict.headline: Preserved at four boundaries, broadened at one.
verdict.detail: CrewAI adds null acceptance to optional fields that the source schema does not declare nullable.

null-acceptance.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP tool schemas distinguishing omission from null.
known_issues: A server may reject explicit null even when omission is valid, creating avoidable validation failures.
null-acceptance.why: Optional and nullable are different contracts. Conflating them lets a downstream caller express values the source never accepted.

tool-icons.title: `icons`
tool-icons.description: An optional array of display icons on a tool definition, each with a source URL, MIME type and size list.
tool-icons.question: Does the tool's icon set reach the agent's tool definition?
tool-icons.notes: Unanimous: a two-entry icon set declared on the fixture's `search_records` tool reaches none of the five capture boundaries, and no framework retains it in metadata either. Two frameworks do model `icons`, but only on resources, never on a tool.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: `crewai_tools` contains no reference to `icons` anywhere in the package, so the field has nowhere to survive adaptation.
notes_by_num.2: LangChain: `langchain_mcp_adapters` contains no reference to `icons`. `StructuredTool.metadata` carries annotations but no icon set.
notes_by_num.3: OpenAI Agents SDK: the `agents` package contains no reference to `icons`. `FunctionTool` keeps `_mcp_title` only.
notes_by_num.4: Pydantic AI: `pydantic_ai.mcp` declares `icons: list[Icon] | None` on its resource type only. `ToolDefinition` has no icon field, so tool icons are dropped.
notes_by_num.5: Mastra: `@mastra/mcp` types `icons` under resource and configuration shapes. No tool type carries it, and `mcpMetadata` holds only the server name and version.

verdict.headline: Destroyed by all five frameworks.
verdict.detail: No adapter exposes an icon set to the agent, and none retains one out of band. Pydantic AI and Mastra model icons for resources but not for tools, so the omission is specific to the tool definition rather than a gap in their MCP typing.

tool-icons.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers declaring tool icons. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
tool-icons.why: Icons are the one part of a tool definition aimed at a human rather than a model. A framework that drops them removes the server's only way to identify its tools visually in any UI built on top of the adapter.

tool-name.description: The identifier a downstream consumer uses to invoke the tool.
tool-name.question: Is the tool name unchanged at each capture boundary?
tool-name.notes: Four frameworks pass the tool name through untouched. One namespaces it with the server key.

notes_by_num.1: Mastra: captured tool actions are namespaced as `<serverKey>_<toolName>`, so `delete_account` becomes `src_delete_account`.

verdict.headline: Unchanged in four frameworks, namespaced in one.
verdict.detail: Prefixing is a transformation rather than a loss, but it changes the exact invocation identifier.

tool-name.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
known_issues: A prefixed name changes between server configurations, so a hard coded allowlist can silently stop matching.
tool-name.why: Name based routing, allowlists, and eval fixtures that match exact tool names break under prefixing.

content-annotations.title: Content `annotations`
content-annotations.description: The `audience`, `priority` and `lastModified` hints that content blocks, resources and prompt messages may carry.
content-annotations.question: Do content annotations survive to the agent?
content-annotations.notes: Annotations say who a block is for and how much it matters. No adapter that delivered the block delivered its annotations. LangChain is unmeasured here: its audio conversion raises on the same result, so the call aborts before this block can be observed. Isolating it needs a fixture that returns one block at a time.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: every content block is dropped, annotations with them.
notes_by_num.2: OpenAI Agents: the text block survives; its annotations do not.
notes_by_num.3: Pydantic AI: the text block survives; its annotations do not.
notes_by_num.4: Mastra: every content block is dropped, annotations with them.

verdict.headline: Absent at every boundary where the block itself survived.
verdict.detail: audience and priority are the server's only way to say 'this part is for the model, this part is for the user'. Nothing downstream can recover them.

content-annotations.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
content-annotations.why: Annotations are how a server says who a piece of content is for and how much it matters. A client that drops them cannot filter assistant-only content out of a user view, cannot prioritise what to keep when context runs short, and cannot sort by recency.

embedded-resource-content.title: Embedded resources
embedded-resource-content.description: A tool result block that inlines a resource's contents together with its URI and MIME type.
embedded-resource-content.question: Does an embedded resource keep its identity, or arrive as anonymous text?
embedded-resource-content.notes: An embedded resource carries its own identity: a uri, a mime type, and contents. No adapter delivers it as a resource. One preserves the fields by stringifying them, one keeps the contents and discards the identity, two drop it. LangChain is unmeasured here: its audio conversion raises on the same result, so the call aborts before this block can be observed. Isolating it needs a fixture that returns one block at a time.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the embedded resource is dropped from the result.
notes_by_num.2: OpenAI Agents: serialized into a text block holding the resource's JSON, so uri and mimeType survive as characters rather than as fields.
notes_by_num.3: Pydantic AI: reduced to a bare text block containing the resource's text. The uri and mimeType that identify it are gone.
notes_by_num.4: Mastra: all content blocks are dropped, embedded resources included.

verdict.headline: Delivered as a resource by none of the five.
verdict.detail: Once the uri is gone the agent cannot cite, re-read, or refer to what it was given.

embedded-resource-content.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
embedded-resource-content.why: The URI and MIME type are what let a caller cite, cache or re-read the content. Stripping them to the inner text leaves the agent holding data it cannot attribute to a source.

resource-link-content.title: `resource_link`
resource-link-content.description: A tool result block that points at a resource URI instead of inlining its contents.
resource-link-content.question: Does a resource link reach the agent as a reference it can follow?
resource-link-content.notes: A resource_link is a pointer the agent is meant to be able to follow. Two adapters keep the pointer but not its type, one of them shedding the name and description on the way. Two drop it entirely. LangChain is unmeasured here: its audio conversion raises on the same result, so the call aborts before this block can be observed. Isolating it needs a fixture that returns one block at a time.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the resource link is dropped from the result.
notes_by_num.2: OpenAI Agents: serialized into a text block holding the link's JSON, so name, uri and description survive as characters rather than as fields.
notes_by_num.3: Pydantic AI: reduced to a bare text block containing only the uri. The link's name and description are gone.
notes_by_num.4: Mastra: all content blocks are dropped, resource links included.

verdict.headline: Survives as text at two boundaries, dropped at two.
verdict.detail: A link flattened into prose still tells the agent where to look, which is more than the alternatives here manage.

resource-link-content.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
resource-link-content.why: Resource links are how a large result stays out of the context window until something asks for it. A framework that flattens the link to text keeps the URI as prose and loses the ability to fetch what it points at.

structured-content.title: `structuredContent`
structured-content.description: A JSON result value returned alongside `content`, conforming to the tool's `outputSchema` when one is declared.
structured-content.question: Does the agent receive the structured value, or only its text rendering?
structured-content.notes: Four of five drop the typed value and pass the agent the text mirror the server sent alongside it, which is the copy meant for humans. Mastra is the exception and keeps structuredContent intact, but it does so by dropping every content block in the same result, so no adapter delivers both halves of the response.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: structuredContent is dropped; only the text mirror reaches the agent.
notes_by_num.2: LangChain: structuredContent is dropped; only the text mirror reaches the agent.
notes_by_num.3: OpenAI Agents: structuredContent is dropped; only the text mirror reaches the agent.
notes_by_num.4: Pydantic AI: structuredContent is dropped; only the text mirror reaches the agent.

verdict.headline: Reaches the agent at one boundary of five, and there by dropping all other content.
verdict.detail: structuredContent exists so an agent can consume a result without parsing prose. Where it is dropped, the typed value a server carefully produced is replaced by its own human-readable summary.

structured-content.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
structured-content.why: The spec asks servers to mirror structured results into a text block for backwards compatibility. That mirror makes a dropped `structuredContent` invisible: the call still looks successful, and typed data quietly becomes a string the model has to re-parse.

tool-audio-content.title: Audio content
tool-audio-content.description: The `audio` content block, carrying base64-encoded audio data and its MIME type.
tool-audio-content.question: Does an audio result survive adaptation?
tool-audio-content.notes: The least survivable content type measured. One adapter passes it through as audio. One turns it into a JSON string. Two drop it. LangChain does something worse than dropping it: it raises, and the exception takes the rest of the result with it, so a server that returns audio alongside text returns nothing usable at all.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the audio block is dropped from the result.
notes_by_num.2: LangChain: raises NotImplementedError -- 'AudioContent conversion to LangChain content blocks is not yet supported' -- which aborts the whole call, so no part of the result reaches the agent.
notes_by_num.3: OpenAI Agents: the block is serialized into a text block containing its JSON, base64 payload and all, so the audio reaches the agent only as characters.
notes_by_num.4: Mastra: all content blocks are dropped, audio included.

verdict.headline: Delivered as audio by one of five; fatal at one.
verdict.detail: An unsupported content type that raises rather than degrades turns a partially supported result into a failed call.

tool-audio-content.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
tool-audio-content.why: Audio is the least-implemented content type in the union, which makes it the sharpest test of whether a framework handles the content list generically or only the cases it happened to code for.

tool-execution-errors.title: `isError`
tool-execution-errors.description: The in-band flag marking a tool result as a tool execution error, which the spec expects clients to pass to the model so it can correct itself.
tool-execution-errors.question: Can the agent tell a tool execution error from a successful result?
tool-execution-errors.notes: Not one of the five hands the agent the boolean the specification defines. Three return the failure as ordinary text, so an agent reading the result cannot tell a failed call from a successful one. Two convert it into an exception, which preserves the fact of failure but moves it out of the result and into control flow.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the failed call returns its text like any other result. Nothing marks it as a failure.
notes_by_num.2: LangChain: the error text arrives as an ordinary text block with a generated lc_ id. The flag is gone.
notes_by_num.3: OpenAI Agents: the error text is returned as normal tool output, indistinguishable from success.
notes_by_num.4: Pydantic AI: converted into a raised ModelRetry rather than a flag on the result. The failure is reachable, but as control flow.
notes_by_num.5: Mastra: converted into a thrown error rather than a flag on the result.

verdict.headline: Delivered by none of the five; two convert it into an exception.
verdict.detail: isError is how a tool says 'this did not work' without the agent having to read prose. Three frameworks erase that distinction entirely.

tool-execution-errors.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
tool-execution-errors.why: MCP separates protocol errors from tool execution errors precisely so a model can retry the second kind with better arguments. A framework that raises both as exceptions, or reports both as success, collapses that distinction and removes the recovery path the spec designed.

tool-image-content.title: Image content
tool-image-content.description: The `image` content block, carrying base64-encoded data and its MIME type.
tool-image-content.question: Does an image result survive adaptation, or is it dropped or flattened to text?
tool-image-content.notes: The two adapters built around multimodal model APIs pass images through; the two that flatten results to text or to structured data drop them. LangChain is unmeasured here: its audio conversion raises on the same result, so the call aborts before this block can be observed. Isolating it needs a fixture that returns one block at a time.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the image block is dropped from the result.
notes_by_num.2: Mastra: all content blocks are dropped, images included.

verdict.headline: Delivered by two, dropped by two, unmeasured at one.
verdict.detail: A tool that returns a chart or a screenshot is only useful if the image reaches a model that can see it.

tool-image-content.usage_note: Not published. Candidate source: count of public MCP servers using this capability. Not estimated, so the panel stays empty until the corpus is scanned.
tool-image-content.why: A dropped image block is a silent failure: the call succeeds, the result arrives, and the payload the tool existed to return is simply gone.

tool-text-content.title: Text content
tool-text-content.description: The `text` content block, the baseline result type that every tool result may carry.
tool-text-content.question: Does text content reach the agent unchanged?
tool-text-content.notes: The one content type almost everything survives. Three adapters pass it through unchanged. CrewAI delivers the characters but wraps them in the repr of the list that held them, so the agent reads brackets and quotes as part of the text. Mastra drops it.

notes_by_num.1: CrewAI: the text arrives stringified inside a Python list repr, as "['SENTINEL_TEXT_BLOCK']" rather than the block's text.
notes_by_num.2: Mastra: all content blocks are dropped, text included; only structuredContent reaches the agent.

verdict.headline: Unchanged at three boundaries, reshaped at one, dropped at one.
verdict.detail: Plain text is the floor. Two of five do not clear it cleanly.

tool-text-content.why: This is the one content type every framework is expected to handle, so it is the control row: the other content types can only be read as losses against a text block that survives.

verdict.headline: Supported by all five.

progress-notifications.description: Server-pushed progress updates for a request that opted in by supplying a progress token, reporting a monotonically increasing value with an optional total and message.

progress-notifications.why: Without it every slow tool is indistinguishable from a hung one, and the only tuning available is the timeout. The client has to send the token first, so this is a capability the framework must actively opt into.

sse-resumability.title: `Last-Event-ID` resumability
sse-resumability.description: Stream resumption in which a client reconnects with the last event id it saw and the server redelivers what it missed.
sse-resumability.question: Does this framework resume a broken stream rather than losing the request?
sse-resumability.notes: No scan produces this row yet, so every cell is unmeasured. It is published because the specification defines the feature, not because anything is known about how these frameworks handle it.

verdict.headline: Not yet measured.
verdict.detail: Break the fixture's response stream mid-call and check whether the adapter reconnects with Last-Event-ID.

sse-resumability.why: Redelivery is the difference between a dropped connection costing nothing and costing an in-flight call. 2026-07-28 removed it, making every broken stream a lost request.
sse-resumability.probe: Break the fixture's response stream mid-call and check whether the adapter reconnects with Last-Event-ID.

transport-streamable-http.title: Streamable HTTP transport
transport-streamable-http.description: One HTTP POST per message to a single endpoint, answered with a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream, and carrying the required `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers.
transport-streamable-http.question: Can the framework talk to a remote server on this revision's terms?
transport-streamable-http.notes: No scan produces this row yet, so every cell is unmeasured. It is published because the specification defines the feature, not because anything is known about how these frameworks handle it.

verdict.headline: Not yet measured.
verdict.detail: Connect each adapter to the fixture over Streamable HTTP and inspect the outgoing headers and stream handling.

transport-streamable-http.why: Every remote MCP server uses this transport, and 2026-07-28 changed it substantially: sessions and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header are gone, SSE resumability is gone, and two new headers are required. An adapter written for the old shape may connect and still be non-conformant.
transport-streamable-http.probe: Connect each adapter to the fixture over Streamable HTTP and inspect the outgoing headers and stream handling.

authorization-oauth.title: OAuth 2.1 authorization
authorization-oauth.description: Transport-level OAuth 2.1 for HTTP transports, including the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter on both authorization and token requests.
authorization-oauth.question: Can the framework authorize against a protected MCP server?
authorization-oauth.notes: No scan produces this row yet, so every cell is unmeasured. It is published because the specification defines the feature, not because anything is known about how these frameworks handle it.

verdict.headline: Not yet measured.
verdict.detail: Point each adapter at an OAuth-protected fixture and inspect the authorization requests it makes.

authorization-oauth.why: Almost every hosted MCP server is protected, so this row decides whether a framework can reach real servers or only local ones. The `resource` parameter is what binds a token to one server; omitting it produces tokens that a careful server will refuse and a careless one will over-accept.
authorization-oauth.probe: Point each adapter at an OAuth-protected fixture and inspect the authorization requests it makes.

authorization-resource-metadata.title: Protected Resource Metadata
authorization-resource-metadata.description: RFC 9728 discovery, where the server advertises its authorization server through a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge and clients follow it rather than being configured by hand.
authorization-resource-metadata.question: Does the framework discover the authorization server from the challenge?
authorization-resource-metadata.notes: No scan produces this row yet, so every cell is unmeasured. It is published because the specification defines the feature, not because anything is known about how these frameworks handle it.

verdict.headline: Not yet measured.
verdict.detail: Return a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge with `resource_metadata` from the fixture and check whether each adapter follows it.

authorization-resource-metadata.why: This is what makes connecting to an unfamiliar protected server possible without out-of-band setup. A framework that requires hand-configured endpoints cannot connect to a server it was not told about in advance, and cannot handle a step-up scope challenge when one arrives.
authorization-resource-metadata.probe: Return a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge with `resource_metadata` from the fixture and check whether each adapter follows it.
